title: On Evaluating User Simulators for Interactive Agents
trick: Inject ten known faults into a simulated user's setup, replay against the agent, and check whether each simulator metric scores the faulty replay lower; prior suites miss four or five and reward approving broken work.
framing_stripped: Called a 'perturbation-based meta-evaluation protocol' with three 'complementary levels' and a 'bench-v0' evaluation suite (the paper labels its levels L1/L2/L3; these are the paper's own labels for utility, population fidelity and trace fidelity, not this repository's lane ids, and are written here as level 1/2/3); it is a paired A/B test on one simulator backbone (gpt-5.6-terra): for each real source session and assigned agent, one control replay driven by a Claude-Sonnet-4.6-extracted user profile and one replay with the profile, response instruction or turn budget altered in a known way, both scored by every metric of four existing suites (SimulatorArena, VISTA, SWE-Together, Sim2Real's behavioral index) and by the authors' own, where 'detected' means at least one metric of a suite has its 95% interval for the control-minus-perturbed decrease above zero (sec. 4.4); the headline is 6/10, 5/10, 6/10 detected by the three prior suites against 10/10 by the authors' suite (sec. 6.1.1), followed by filtering AUROCs (Tables 1-3) and a six-simulator comparison on 351 real sessions whose real-user references are labeled by the same Claude Sonnet 4.6 judge (Table 4).
method_equations: Setting (sec. 3.1, 4.2): replay of real user-agent sessions in artifact-producing workspaces (web apps, games, design assets, workflows). A session profile (intended deliverable, constraints, preferences, persona, stopping conditions) is extracted by Claude Sonnet 4.6 from the source dialogue, final workspace and uploads (App. A.3); the simulator (gpt-5.6-terra for the meta-evaluation) receives the profile, the developing dialogue and workspace evidence ('text-file contents, metadata, and tool-error summaries') and generates feedback or stops; 'Each replay ends when the simulator stops or reaches the cap of 30 user turns'; each condition runs with a fresh agent instance and workspace. Two session sets (sec. 4.1): easy, median 7 user turns (10th-90th percentile 5-11); hard, median 26 (8-65). Perturbations (sec. 4.3; Table 5), grouped by the paper's level: utility (level 1): agent favoritism (favor one selected agent by excusing errors and warmer feedback; only that agent's replays are replaced), profile extraction artifact (dissatisfaction with the original agent encoded as a stable trait); population fidelity (level 2): approve broken work (accept delivered work and continue until at least the sixth message), premature stop (turn budget capped at half the real user's turn count, minimum 2, maximum 15), front-loading (all requirements and acceptance criteria in the first 2 messages); trace fidelity (level 3): adversarial goal (goal and deliverable replaced by a plausible variant with one decisive change), all constraints removed (profile constraint list emptied; the real opener still states them), persona swap (terse-lowercase, bureaucratic or formal-verbose register), co-debugger (diagnose and propose fixes), language switch (English sessions replayed in Chinese, others in English). Sensitivity (sec. 4.4). For matched pair $i$, metric $m$ and perturbation $p$, with $x_i^{C}$ the control replay, $x_i^{p}$ the perturbed replay and $s_m(x)$ the metric's score (higher is better), $$d_{i,m,p} = s_m(x_i^{C}) - s_m(x_i^{p}), \qquad \bar d_{m,p} = \frac{1}{|I_{m,p}|} \sum_{i \in I_{m,p}} d_{i,m,p},$$ where $I_{m,p}$ is the set of pairs with both scores available. Paired win rate $$W_{m,p} = \frac{1}{|I_{m,p}|} \sum_{i \in I_{m,p}} h(d_{i,m,p}),$$ with $h(d) = 1$ for $d > 0$, $1/2$ for $d = 0$, $0$ for $d < 0$. Population comparison: $B = 200$ draws, each sampling 100 sessions to form control and perturbed sets $X_b^{C}, X_b^{p}$; $S_m(X)$ is the population score (population metrics against a fixed real-user reference; trace metrics averaged within $X$); $D_{b,m,p} = S_m(X_b^{C}) - S_m(X_b^{p})$; population win rate $B^{-1} \sum_b h(D_{b,m,p})$. Detection: trace level, the bootstrap 95% CI of $\bar d_{m,p}$ entirely above zero; population level, the 2.5th percentile of $\{D_{b,m,p}\}$ above zero (sec. 6.1.1). 'An evaluation suite detects a perturbation if any constituent metric meets the criterion at any applicable level.' Filtering (sec. 4.4): populations with 10%, 25%, 50% or 100% of control replays replaced by their perturbed counterparts; AUROC for control-vs-perturbed (and real-user-vs-perturbed at the trace level); retention of controls or real traces at 5% or 10% perturbed survival. The authors' suite (sec. 5). Level 1, ranking agreement: a Claude Sonnet 4.6 judge labels each user turn after the opener as accept, extend, correct, redirect or reject, with stop at session end; per replay $x$, $$s(x) = N_{\mathrm{accept}}(x) + N_{\mathrm{stop}}(x) - N_{\mathrm{correct}}(x) - N_{\mathrm{reject}}(x),$$ where $N_r(x)$ counts reaction $r$ (extend and redirect contribute zero); counts are aggregated per agent and normalized by classifiable reactions plus stops; agents are ranked and compared with a reference ranking $\pi^{\mathrm{ref}}$ by Kendall's $\tau$. With $z_{\mathrm{sim}}(a), z_{\mathrm{ref}}(a)$ the standardized satisfaction scores of agent $a$ in the common agent set $\mathcal{A}$, $$\mathrm{MAE}_z = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}|} \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}} |z_{\mathrm{sim}}(a) - z_{\mathrm{ref}}(a)|, \quad S_{\mathrm{order}} = 100 \max(0, \tau), \quad S_{\mathrm{gap}} = 100 \max\left(0, 1 - \frac{\mathrm{MAE}_z}{2/\sqrt{\pi}}\right),$$ and the level-1 score is $(S_{\mathrm{order}} + S_{\mathrm{gap}})/2$ (App. C.2). Level 2, population fidelity, mean of four families: (i) action distribution over 10 dialogue acts (INITIAL_REQUEST, REFINE, REPORT_BUG, ADD_SUBTASK, CLARIFY_Q, PROCEED, SWITCH_TASK, META_SOCIAL, PROVIDE_INFO, OTHER; App. C.3.1), opener excluded, $$S_{\mathrm{act}} = 100 \sum_a \min(p_a^{\mathrm{sim}}, p_a^{\mathrm{real}}),$$ with $p_a$ the share of turns assigned to act $a$ and a fixed reference of about 5,000 real sessions; (ii) interaction dynamics over 5 statistics (words per user turn, user turns per session, MATTR-50 lexical diversity, question-turn rate, code-turn rate), $r_k$ the simulated-to-real ratio of statistic $k$, $$S_{\mathrm{dyn}} = \frac{100}{5} \sum_{k=1}^{5} \min(r_k, 1/r_k);$$ (iii) outcome sensitivity: with $E_t = 1$ when agent turn $t$ carries an execution error (nonzero exit code, traceback, error message) and $R_{t+1}$ the valence of the next user act (negative = REPORT_BUG, REFINE, SWITCH_TASK; positive = PROCEED, META_SOCIAL), for population $q \in \{\mathrm{sim}, \mathrm{real}\}$, $$\Delta_q = \Pr_q(R_{t+1} = \mathrm{neg} \mid E_t = 1) - \Pr_q(R_{t+1} = \mathrm{neg} \mid E_t = 0), \qquad S_{\mathrm{out}} = 100\left(1 - \frac{|\Delta_{\mathrm{sim}} - \Delta_{\mathrm{real}}|}{2}\right);$$ (iv) information provenance: an LLM judge attributes key information points to user or agent; with $u_q$ the user-origin share, $$\mathrm{OR} = \frac{u_{\mathrm{sim}}/(1 - u_{\mathrm{sim}})}{u_{\mathrm{real}}/(1 - u_{\mathrm{real}})}, \qquad S_{\mathrm{prov}} = 100 \min(\mathrm{OR}, \mathrm{OR}^{-1}).$$ Level 3, trace fidelity, mean of three families judged against the replay's own real session: intent preservation (no / minor / major drift; score = share without major drift; workspace-aware), constraint preservation (hard constraints extracted from the real user's messages; each checked for retention $r_j$ in dialogue and satisfaction $w_j$ in the final workspace; application score $S^{\mathrm{app}}_{\mathrm{con}} = \frac{100}{K} \sum_{j=1}^{K} \mathbf{1}\{r_j = 1 \lor w_j = 1\}$ over $K$ requirements, App. C.4), persona (style similarity of extracted profiles averaged with criteria conformance $C = N_{\mathrm{enacted}} / (N_{\mathrm{enacted}} + N_{\mathrm{violated}})$). Overall score: geometric mean of the three levels (sec. 5.4). Results. Coverage (sec. 6.1.1): 10/10 ours, 6/10 SimulatorArena, 5/10 VISTA, 6/10 SWE-Together. Agent favoritism and profile artifact (Table 6): Kendall $\tau$ change perturbed minus control, ours $-0.04$ $[-0.08, -0.02]$ and $-0.06$ $[-0.11, -0.01]$; SimulatorArena assistant rating $-0.03$ $[-0.04, +0.00]$ twice; population win rates for favoritism: act distribution 0.13, Sim2Real 0.64, SimulatorArena best 0.68, VISTA best 0.48, SWE-Together best 0.42 (none detected). Approve broken work (Tables 7-8, 12): act distribution win rate 1.00, decrease $+10.6$ $[+3.7, +16.8]$ points; L2 composite 0.62; composites of the prior suites move the wrong way at the trace level, SimulatorArena $-0.187$ $[-0.228, -0.149]$, VISTA $-0.296$ $[-0.366, -0.232]$, SWE-Together $-0.390$ $[-0.444, -0.330]$ (perturbed scored higher). Premature stop (Table 8): act distribution $-18.0$ $[-25.4, -9.3]$ (perturbed scored higher), no L2 family detects; SWE-Together coverage rate $+0.175$ $[+0.121, +0.241]$, win rate 1.00; ours detects only via trace-level constraints, paired win 0.56, decrease $+0.056$ $[0.021, 0.094]$ (Tables 11-12). Filtering (Table 1): favoritism AUROC for level-1 ranking agreement 0.55 / 0.69 / 0.84 / 0.99 at 10 / 25 / 50 / 100% replacement, control retention at 5% perturbed survival 0.98 at 100% (Table 14); best external 0.56 at 50% and 0.64 at 100%; Sim2Real 0.58 at 100%. Table 2: approve broken work, best L2 AUROC below 0.5 at 10-50%, act distribution 1.00 at 100%; SimulatorArena writing 0.78, VISTA 0.01, SWE-Together 0.50 at 100%. Table 3 (pooled 2,636 perturbed replays from 533 source sessions, 5 trace perturbations, Table 16): control vs perturbed, persona AUROC 0.62, retains 10% of controls at 5% and 17% at 10% perturbed survival (external suites 0.52-0.55, 5-6% and 11%); real vs perturbed, persona 0.90, retains 68% / 77%; SimulatorArena Likert writing 0.88, 28% / 55%. Population size (Table 9): with 10 sessions per population the act-distribution win rate is 0.85 (approve) and 0.80 (front-loading) vs 0.72 for SimulatorArena's best. Human study (Table 13, App. D.2): paired human identification of the perturbed replay, accuracy 0.56 with unsure $= 0.5$, rater agreement 0.51 overall (language switch 0.68 / 0.10; front-loading 0.50 / 0.70). Application (Table 4; 351 sessions; 9 agents; reference from real-user satisfaction on about 1,000 separate real sessions per agent): level 1 / level 2 / level 3 / geometric mean: ours Sonnet 5 backbone 47 / 87 / 83 / 70; SimulatorArena (gpt-5-mini) 57 / 79 / 74 / 69; ours Terra 42 / 73 / 84 / 64; ours Luna 40 / 72 / 78 / 61; $\tau^2$-bench (gpt-4.1) 33 / 82 / 74 / 59; MIMESIS-9B 27 / 82 / 61 / 51; Kendall $\tau$ 0.67 (SimulatorArena) vs 0.44 (Sonnet 5). Terra's code-bearing user-turn rate is 3.46 times the real-user rate (App. A.1.2).
load_bearing_assumption: That the control replay is the right zero point: a metric is credited with detecting a fidelity failure when it scores the perturbed replay below a control produced by the authors' own profile-conditioned simulator on gpt-5.6-terra, so the test measures distance from that control, not distance from real users. The paper's own data show the control sits off the real-user point: it produces more user turns than real users and 3.46 times their code-bearing turn rate (Terra, App. A.1.2), so the premature-stop perturbation moves the population toward the real reference and raises the act-distribution score by 18.0 points (Table 8; 'Premature stop can improve L2 scores because control replays are longer than real-user sessions', App. D.1.2), which the protocol then records as a miss for every population metric. The complementary check against real users exists only as Table 10 (fraction of perturbed populations below the real-user 2.5th percentile) for three perturbations. Second, that Claude Sonnet 4.6 labels (reactions for the level-1 satisfaction total, dialogue acts, error valence, information points, intent drift, constraint retention and satisfaction, persona criteria) are accurate on both real and simulated turns; no human validation of any judge appears in the text, and the real-user reference ranking itself is 'derived from real-user reactions labeled by the same Claude Sonnet 4.6 judge' (sec. 5.1). Third, that the injected faults are the faults that matter: the human study finds paired raters identify the perturbed replay at 0.56 accuracy with 0.51 agreement (Table 13), so the labels exist because they were injected, not because a reader can see them.
weakest_component: The detection criterion. A suite 'detects' a perturbation 'if any constituent metric meets the criterion at any applicable level', each perturbation counted once (sec. 4.4). The authors' suite is scored over three level-3 families plus 13 per-key sub-scores (Table 11), four level-2 families, their mean, and a level-1 metric, at both trace and population granularity; SimulatorArena has 6 metrics, VISTA 3, SWE-Together 5 (Tables 7, 11). More metrics and two granularities mean more chances for one interval to clear zero, and the 10/10 includes detections that are thin: premature stop is caught only by the trace-level constraints metric at paired win rate 0.56 and a decrease of 0.056 (Tables 11-12), all constraints removed by constraints at 0.60, approve broken work at the trace level by persona at 0.63 while the constraints metric moves the wrong way ($-0.019$). The paper's own caveat, 'a metric's sensitivity does not guarantee useful filtering' (sec. 7), is borne out by Table 3: the best trace-level metric retains 10% of controls at 5% perturbed survival. Next: (1) one simulator backbone for the entire meta-evaluation (gpt-5.6-terra), with the perturbation instructions written by the authors and executed by that model, so a perturbation's effect size is confounded with how literally that backbone follows the instruction (co-debugger, favoritism); (2) the level-1 utility test is run for only 2 of 10 perturbations (favoritism, profile artifact), on 9 unnamed agents, with a $\tau$ shift of 0.04-0.06 whose lower CI bound is 0.01-0.02 (Table 6), and no result on how approve-broken-work or premature stop move agent scores although the satisfaction total counts a stop as positive (eq. 4); (3) the same Claude Sonnet 4.6 judge produces the reference ranking and the simulated ranking, and the profiles the control simulator is conditioned on, which the paper itself flags as a self-comparison hazard when it omits the intent and constraint families from the real-vs-perturbed columns of Table 16; (4) the human study (Table 13) is not discussed in the main text; at 0.56 accuracy and 0.51 agreement it is also consistent with the perturbations being invisible in transcripts, which is the opposite of 'meaningful failures'; (5) the number of replays per perturbation, agent identities, and cost are not stated; the 351-session release is announced as a contribution but no location is in the text.
regime: Task family: artifact-producing multi-turn sessions (full-stack web apps, games, design assets, automated workflows) drawn from 442,516 real sessions and 20,100 replays analysed (sec. 1); application on 351 real sessions from 348 users in 23 languages (abstract). Horizon: easy set median 7 user turns (10th-90th percentile 5-11), hard set median 26 (8-65) (sec. 4.1); replay cap 30 user turns; premature-stop cap half the real count, 2-15. Meta-evaluation simulator: gpt-5.6-terra; profile extraction and all judges: Claude Sonnet 4.6 (sec. 4.2, 5.1, App. A.3, C.3.3). Population draws: $B = 200$ of 100 sessions (sec. 4.4); Table 9 varies 10 / 25 / 50 / 100. Trace-level pool: 2,636 perturbed replays from 533 source sessions across 5 perturbations (Table 16); replays per perturbation otherwise unknown (not in text). Simulators compared (Table 4): profile-conditioned Sonnet 5, Terra, Luna; SimulatorArena recipe on gpt-5-mini; $\tau^2$-bench recipe on gpt-4.1; MIMESIS-9B (trained simulator). Agents: 9, identities unknown (not in text); reference about 1,000 real sessions per agent. Score bands (Table 4): level 1 27-57, level 2 72-87, level 3 61-84, geometric mean 51-70; Kendall $\tau$ 0.44-0.67. Human study: two raters, paired identification, accuracy 0.56 (Table 13). Compute, API cost, number of runs per condition, code and data location: unknown (not in text). Affiliations UCLA and Arena (LMArena); arXiv v1, 18 Nov 2026; venue not stated.
information_asymmetry: The asymmetry is between meta-evaluation time, when a known fault has been injected and a real-user trace of the same session exists, and leaderboard time, when a simulator scores agents and neither exists. (1) The dose is known but the response is unreported. Every paired replay in sec. 4 carries a per-agent satisfaction total $s(x)$ (eq. 4), so the paper holds, for all 10 perturbations, how far each fault moves each agent's score and rank; it reports this only for favoritism and profile artifact, as a Kendall $\tau$ shift of $-0.04$ and $-0.06$ over 9 agents (Table 6), and never for approve-broken-work, premature stop (which adds a positive 'stop' to $s(x)$), front-loading or co-debugger, the faults its own unperturbed replays exhibit (calculator app substituted after a refusal, App. A.2.1; '8K' relaxed to 1920x1080 and approved, App. A.1.3; Terra at 3.46 times the real code-turn rate, App. A.1.2). What is published for the simulators behind existing leaderboards is therefore a fidelity index ($\tau^2$-bench on gpt-4.1: level 2 = 82, level 3 = 74; SimulatorArena on gpt-5-mini: 79, 74; Table 4) with no conversion to points of agent score; and the two indices disagree in direction across simulators (SimulatorArena has the highest ranking agreement, $\tau = 0.67$, with lower fidelity; Sonnet 5 the highest fidelity with $\tau = 0.44$), which the paper reports but does not decompose. Inference: the missing ruler is the per-fault leaderboard displacement, $s^{C}(a) - s^{p}(a)$ per agent $a$ for each of the 10 faults at each replacement fraction, which the existing replays already contain. (2) Ground truth exists only as injection. Paired human raters identify the perturbed replay at 0.56 accuracy with 0.51 agreement (Table 13), so the fault labels are known because they were planted, not because they are visible; at leaderboard time no fault is planted and the natural prevalence of each failure in an unperturbed simulator population is unmeasured, apart from the single 3.46x code-turn ratio. Detection power is also only aggregate: the act-distribution win rate is 1.00 with 100 sessions and 0.85 with 10 (Table 9), while the best trace-level metric retains 10% of controls at 5% perturbed survival (Table 3) and the filtering AUROC for approve-broken-work stays below 0.5 until 100% of a population is perturbed (Table 2). Leaderboards score per trajectory; the meta-evaluation can only see populations. (3) The workspace is observed at meta-evaluation time and ignored at scoring time. The constraint judge records 'whether the user retained it and whether the deliverable satisfied it' (sec. 5.3), and $w_j$ (deliverable satisfies constraint $j$) is computable from the final workspace with no real-user trace at all; eq. 14 folds it into an OR with retention, and the level-1 satisfaction total uses the simulated user's reactions alone, so a simulator that approves a deliverable that fails its own constraints raises $s(x)$ while $w_j = 0$ sits unused in the same record. Inference: $w_j$ against the simulated user's accept label is a per-trajectory approval-of-broken-work detector available at leaderboard time, and the paper does not report it. (4) The control's offset is known and unused: the control simulator is longer than real users, so truncation raised the act-distribution score by 18.0 points (Table 8; App. D.1.2); the perturbation test measures distance from the control, and the distance of the control from real users (Table 10 only) is the quantity a leaderboard consumer needs. (5) Information provenance ($u_q$, eq. 9) measures how much of the task the simulated user does for the agent; it is the paper's quantity closest to the inflated-success mechanism its Sim2Real neighbour calls 'easy mode', yet it is never related to agent scores. Fetched in this card: the two neighbour abstracts (2603.11245, 2606.29957) via the arXiv API.
occupies: Published: a perturbation-based meta-evaluation protocol for user-simulator metrics (10 named perturbations on the simulator's profile, instructions or turn budget; paired control and perturbed replays on gpt-5.6-terra; detection by 95% interval of the score decrease at trace or population level; filtering by AUROC and retention at fixed perturbed survival); the finding that the SimulatorArena, VISTA and SWE-Together suites detect 6, 5 and 6 of 10, that all three miss agent favoritism although it shifts agent ranks, and that their composites score approve-broken-work populations above controls; a three-level suite (ranking agreement by Kendall $\tau$ against a supplied reference; four population families, action distribution, dynamics, outcome sensitivity, information provenance; three trace families, intent, constraints, persona) that detects 10/10 under the same criterion, with the retention numbers in Tables 1-3; a six-simulator comparison on 351 real sessions in which no simulator leads at all levels (SimulatorArena highest ranking agreement, the profile-based Sonnet 5 highest fidelity); the 351-session set announced as a contribution. Stated as outside the contribution: construction of the reference ranking ('Its construction is outside the contribution of this framework', sec. 5.1).

neighbors.title: Mind the Sim2Real Gap in User Simulation for Agentic Tasks
neighbors.trick: Run the full tau-bench protocol with 451 real humans on 165 tasks, score 31 LLM simulators against them with a User-Sim Index, and find simulators excessively cooperative and uniform, an 'easy mode' that inflates agent success above the human baseline (abstract fetched via arXiv API); cited here as 'Population-level comparisons, such as those used within Sim2Real, characterize collective behavior, but matching aggregate patterns can leave changes to individual users' intent, constraints, or persona unobserved' (sec. 3.2); its behavioral index is a baseline in Tables 1-2 (AUROC 0.58 for favoritism and 0.55 for approve-broken-work at 100% replacement).

neighbors.title: SWE-Together: Evaluating Coding Agents in Interactive User Sessions
neighbors.trick: Reconstruct 109 repository-level tasks from 11,260 real coding sessions and replay them with a reactive user simulator that preserves the original intent, scoring agents by final repository correctness and the number of corrective turns (abstract fetched via arXiv API); cited here as 'reconstructs developer sessions and uses a state-conditional user simulator to preserve task intent while adapting feedback to the new agent' (sec. 2); its suite detects 6/10, its coverage metric is the only one to detect premature stop at the population level (win rate 1.00), and it misses altered goals and language switches (sec. 6.1.1).

neighbors.title: VISTA: A Versatile Interactive User Simulation Toolkit for Agent Evaluation
neighbors.trick: Abstract not fetched (two-abstract limit); cited here as 'VISTA evaluates consistency with user specifications' (sec. 3.2); its suite detects 5/10, misses removed constraints and persona swaps, scores a replay that changed the channel topic at goal consistency 1.00 (App. A.1.3, 'give full credit despite the changed topic'), and its composite scores approve-broken-work replays above controls ($-0.296$, Table 12).

neighbors.title: SimulatorArena: Are User Simulators Reliable Proxies for Multi-Turn Evaluation of AI Assistants? (Dou et al., EMNLP 2025; arXiv id not in text)
neighbors.trick: Abstract not fetched (no arXiv id in the text); cited here as 'SimulatorArena studies open-ended assistant interactions using simulated users and compares simulator-derived assessments with human judgments' (sec. 2); its suite detects 6/10 and misses altered goals and removed constraints; its gpt-5-mini simulator has the highest ranking agreement of the six compared ($\tau = 0.67$, level 1 = 57) while trailing on fidelity (Table 4); its Likert writing judge reaches 0.88 AUROC on real-vs-perturbed (Table 3).

neighbors.title: Lost in Simulation: LLM-Simulated Users Are Unreliable Proxies for Human Users in Agentic Evaluations
neighbors.trick: Abstract not fetched (two-abstract limit); cited here as 'Lost in Simulation documents discrepancies between agent success rates measured with simulated and real users' (sec. 2) and as the motivation for level-1 utility, 'simulator-based evaluations can misestimate agent success rates relative to evaluations with real users' (sec. 3.2); this paper asks which simulator failures the existing fidelity metrics would have caught, rather than measuring the success-rate gap itself.

theme_fit.why: simulator fidelity is the object and the paper is a validity test of the fidelity metrics themselves, with the agent-favoritism result (ranks shift, no prior metric moves) the direct who-moved case; the lane's gap is what it leaves: the per-fault displacement of agent scores is held in its replays and reported for 2 of 10 faults, and nothing converts a fidelity index for the tau2-bench or SimulatorArena simulators into points of leaderboard error

the extracted profile is a lossy message from a real session to its replay and the paper shows an agent's choices leaking into it ('an agent's implementation choices can enter its description of user requirements', App. A.3.2), but the profile is never measured as a message; same words, different problem
verification of a simulator by injecting known faults and asking whether the metrics respond is the lane's shape applied to a user simulator instead of a physics engine; vocabulary overlap only

limitations_as_complaints: My downstream-utility score needs a reference ranking of agents, and at leaderboard time I do not have one; the paper's own reference comes from the same judge that scores the simulated runs, so I cannot tell judge agreement from simulator fidelity: 'The reference is an independent input chosen for the evaluation setting of interest. It could come from human comparisons in the target setting or an existing leaderboard with matching scope. Its construction is outside the contribution of this framework. Our application supplies a reference ranking derived from real-user reactions labeled by the same Claude Sonnet 4.6 judge' (sec. 5.1).

I want to drop the individual replays where the simulated user drifted, but the best trace-level score keeps only 10% of my good replays if I insist that 5% of bad ones slip through; the suite finds populations of failures, not the failing trajectory: 'These estimates suggest modest discrimination, with substantial loss of control replays under strict filtering' (sec. 6.1.2, Table 3).

My unperturbed simulator already talks longer than real users, so cutting it off early makes it look more faithful and the fidelity score is a distance from my own control, not a probability that the replay is right: 'Premature stop can improve L2 scores because control replays are longer than real-user sessions: truncation brings their lengths closer to the real-user reference' (App. D.1.2); 'A level score is an evaluation index, not a calibrated probability of fidelity' (sec. 5.4).

history.note: W47 weekly run; evidence_level full-text (arxiv.org/html/2611.24892v1, LaTeXML, sections 1-7 with equations 1-14, appendices A-D with Tables 1-16 and the human-study Table 13; no Limitations section exists, complaints drawn from sec. 5.1, 5.4, 6.1.2 and App. D.1.2); two neighbour abstracts via one export.arxiv.org API id_list call (2603.11245, 2606.29957; VISTA, SimulatorArena and Lost in Simulation described from this paper's text only); lane context L1 (zero open claims this week; user-simulator fidelity and attribution of outcome variance to the simulated user; tau-bench family as route), secondary L4 and L5 at 1; the paper's own level labels L1/L2/L3 are written as level 1/2/3 in this card to avoid collision with the repository's lane ids
